newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: CENTURY ZINC TO SEEK ADJOURNMENT OF ARBITRATION TODAY
Mining company Century Zinc says it will seek an adjournment of the Native Title Tribunal hearings due to begin in Mt Isa today because it's close to reaching a settlement with all parties involved.
Arbitration on the billion dollar project began after five years of negotiations between the company and Gulf Aboriginal communities failed earlier this year.

But Century Zinc now claims it's gained the support of all 12 native title claimants involved in the project. The company says it's informed Queensland Premier of the support, but the Government is yet to receive confirming documentation.

Century Zinc has put its 60-million dollar compansation package back on offer, and Premier Rob Borbidge says if the support's confirmed, consideration will be given to renewing its 30-million dollar infrastructure package.
20,000 BHP WORKERS COULD STRIKE ON WEDNESDAY
Up to 20,000 BHP workers around Australia could strike on Wednesday in sympathy for colleagues who'll lose their jobs because of BHP's decision to end steelmaking in Newcastle.

Last week BHP decided to end integrated steelmaking in the city in 1999, a move which could see 2,500 thousand jobs go. Unions have vowed to continue to pressure on BHP, and will meet with the ACTU in Sydney today to plan the industrial campaign.

Meanwhile, BHP Chairman Brian Loton, the company's Chief Executive John Prescott and head of the Steel Division, Ron McNeilly, will visit the Newcastle Steelworks today. And it's expected unions will seize that opportunity to express their anger at the decision.
FIRST ABORIGINAL WOMENS LEGAL CENTRE OPENS

The country's first Aboriginal Women's Legal Centre has been opened in Sydney. Attorney General Jeff Shaw says aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women have traditionally experienced problems in getting access to legal advice.

He says they've had difficulties in getting assistance that is culturally sensitive and gender specific. The new Centre will provide them with legal advice, information and eventually, representation.
SA WANTS RAIL LINK COMMITMENT IN FEDERAL BUDGET

The South Australian Premier says he wants a commitment in the Federal Budget for the proposed Adelaide to Darwin rail link. Premier John Olsen says the Adelaide-to-Darwin rail link is the best option for Australia.

He says the project has already passed environmental and legislative hurdles, unlike the Melbourne to Darwin proposal which has no cost estimates, or feasibility studies. He says it also lacks financial planning and a timetable for construction. The South Australian and Northern Territory Governments have pledged A$100 million each toward the project. And now Mr Olsen says it's time for the Federal Government to approve infrastructure borrowing arrangements in its budget to ensure the 86-year-old dream finally becomes a reality.
The Premier says BHP's 70-million dollar commitment to Whyalla's steel industry has also secured the project's future.
FLOODING IN NORTHER TASMANIA
Prolongued steady rain across Northern Tasmania has swollen rivers and streams and caused flooding in some areas, although it has been welcomed by farmers.

Flooding in the Meander River basin has forced the evacuation of several homes in the low-lying area of Deloraine near the town's caravan park. Although the rain has now stopped, the Meander River is expected to rise further.

There's a flood warning for the Mersey River, and many rivers in the North East have broken their banks. Some parts of the North East have recorded more than 120 millimetres since the rain started last Thursday night.
ROUND-THE-WORLD YACHT RACE RESCUERS THANKED

The Australian rescuers of two sailors in the Vendee Globe round-the-world yacht race have joined the winners in France in receiving awards. Thousands of people gathered in the French port of Sables d'Olonne to honour air force Colonel Yann Person and navy Captain Rowan Moffitt, for the rescue of Britain's Tony Bullimore and Frenchman, Thierry Dubois.
In addition to the awards, the pair were made honorary citizens of the French city, which plans to rename one of its main streets Adelaide, after the Australian frigate that rescued the sailors.

Frenchman Christophe Auguin won the race and broke the solo round-the-world sailing record. In all, three sailors were rescued during the event and one contestant, Canadian Gerry Rouf, was lost at sea.
FRASER SLAMS HANSON'S IDEALS AS REPUGNANT
Former Prime Minister, Malcolm Fraser, says Federal Independent MP Pauline Hanson's One Nation Party is based on racism, fear, prejudice and downright ignorance.

Speaking at a Melbourne function last night, Mr Fraser said civilised Australians would reject the new party. He said Ms Hanson's opposition to immigration is unfounded, saying Australia should be looking to boost immigration.

Mr Fraser described the ideals behind One Nation as repugnant, and called on Australians to stand up for Australian values. He said there is a danger that the movement could divide Australia, and damage the nation's place on the world stage.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
